newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mayors oppose new clean air rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mayors oppose new clean air rules.

text.p: U.S. mayors voted Tuesday to oppose a plan by the Environmental Protection Agency to set strict new limits on smog and soot, saying the proposed standards could jeopardise local economies.

The U.S. Conference of Mayors, meeting in San Francisco, approved the controversial resolution after a brief debate. The resolution, introduced by Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer, faced little opposition.
"I don't think there's a mayor anywhere that doesn't want clean air," Archer told the conference during debate. "In this instance, I think we've gone too far too fast."
The resolution calls for the EPA to stick with current standards for smog-forming ozone and fine particles rather than tightening them as it proposed last November.
Environmental groups criticised the conference vote.
"There's a lot more support (for the standards) than this sad little vote would indicate," said Kathryn Hohmann, director of environmental quality for the Sierra Club.
She added; "We think that the industry scare tactics had sunk in the minds of the mayors."
The American Lung Association called the vote "disappointing."
"We really feel they should be more concerned with the health of citizens and children," said Anne Casanova, a spokeswoman for the San Francisco arm of the association.
The White House is considering the EPA plan, which has sparked strong opposition from Republicans and Democratic lawmakers from cities that depend on steel, car, and fossil fuel industries.
However, other lawmakers are urging the White House to stand by EPA's plan.
Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato Tuesday told President Clinton tighter standards are needed to help areas like New York that are downwind of lightly controlled pollution sources in the Midwest.
"Asthma is the third ranking cause of hospitalization for children under 15," he said in a June 24 letter to Clinton. "That is why it is so important to support these new EPA clean air standards."

If the proposal which EPA is expected to finalise in the next few days goes through, hundreds of counties that now meet air quality standards will be forced to take additional measures to remain in compliance.
If an area does not meet new standards, it could eventually be subject to strict sanctions, including the loss of highway funds, opponents of the measure have warned.
Mayors at the conference called the new standards unfunded mandates, and said they opposed them because they could hinder efforts to attract businesses to urban areas and undermine economic growth.

"The proposed standards have the potential to jeopardise progress toward other federal priorities that are equally important to achieving sustainable communities, such as the revitalisation of our cities, empowerment zone initiatives, job creation and improved technologies," the Conference of Mayors resolution said.
Only one mayor opposed Archer's resolution during the debate.
"I've been convinced ... that there are enough deaths from this level of particulate matter that the standard makes sense," Richmond, Calif., Mayor Rosemary Corbin told the conference.
The Sierra Club said the EPA plan could be costly, but over time would benefit cities by improving the quality of life and cutting health care costs related to respiratory illnesses.
